stories.summary: US Vice President JD Vance has publicly distanced himself from President Donald Trump’s defence of the Iran war after the Republican Party suffered major losses in the midterm elections. Vance blamed the unpopular conflict for the GOP’s poor performance, arguing voters rejected the party over issues including the war, cost of living and foreign policy.

stories.headline: PSA can’t bypass criminal law: HC
stories.title: PSA can’t bypass criminal law: HC
stories.summary: Srinagar, Nov 04: The High Court of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh has quashed the preventive detention of a Pulwama resident booked under the Public Safety Act (PSA), observing that extraordinary powers of preventive detention cannot be used as a substitute for ordinary criminal proceedings or to bypass safeguards available under criminal law. The court directed the authorities to release Ajaz Ahmad Seh, a resident of Sehpora in Rajpora, Pulwama, forthwith, provided his custody is not required in connection with any other case or under any other lawful order. Justice Wasim Sadiq Nargal passed the judgment while allowing a habeas corpus petition challenging detention order No. 34/DMP/PSA/2025 dated July 28, 2025, issued by the District Magistrate, Pulwama, under Section 8 of the Jammu and Kashmir Public Safety Act. According to the grounds of detention, Seh was allegedly in contact with a Pakistan-based terrorist handler affiliated with Jaish-e-Mohammad through telephone and the encrypted application Zangi, accessed using a virtual private network (VPN). He was also accused of functioning as an Over Ground Worker (OGW) by allegedly providing food, shelter, clothing, transportation and information to active terrorists, including Haris Nazir of Kachipora, Rajpora. The police dossier further alleged that he shared information about the movement of security forces and encouraged local youth to join terrorist organisations. However, the High Court observed that despite the seriousness of the allegations, the detention grounds lacked specific particulars, including the dates of alleged communications, the nature of information exchanged and the particular acts through which logistical assistance was allegedly provided. The court held that merely asserting that a person used an encrypted application or remained in contact with individuals allegedly associated with terrorist organisations was insufficient, without relevant supporting material, to justify curtailing personal liberty through preventive detention. "Preventive detention legislation cannot be permitted to become an instrument for bypassing the safeguards of the ordinary criminal process," the court observed. It further said that if the investigating agency possessed evidence of electronic communications, assistance to terrorists or sharing of security-force movements, the allegations could have been investigated under applicable criminal laws, including the Unlawful Activities (Prevention) Act, 1967, subject to the ingredients of the offences being satisfied. The court also questioned the District Magistrate's independent application of mind, noting that a comparison of the police dossier and detention grounds revealed substantial reproduction of allegations. It observed that the detaining authority was required to independently evaluate the material rather than mechanically adopt the police narrative. Citing Supreme Court judgments, including Rekha v. State of Tamil Nadu and Vijay Narain Singh v. State of Bihar, the High Court reiterated that preventive detention is an extraordinary measure and must be exercised sparingly and strictly within constitutional and statutory safeguards. "The Court does not minimise the seriousness of allegations involving terrorist organisations or activities prejudicial to the security of the State," Justice Nargal observed, adding that a balance must be maintained between national security and personal liberty. The court ultimately held that the detention order suffered from material legal infirmities and quashed it, directing Seh's immediate release, subject to there being no other lawful restraint on his custody.

stories.headline: Supreme Court says it cannot interfere in criteria for SC/ST reserved constituencies
stories.title: Supreme Court says it cannot interfere in criteria for SC/ST reserved constituencies
reasons: corroboration: single independent source -> medium confidence
event term: 'supreme court' in title weight 44
article_sentences: 'Can't interfere in norms for SC/ST seats in house'NEW DELHI: Refusing to blur the constitutional 'Lakshman Rekha' that separates the three organs of governance, Supreme Court Wednesday said it cannot usurp legislature's exclusive powers to interfere in the criteria for reserving an assembly or parliamentary constituency for Scheduled Castes or Scheduled Tribes." We cannot become the third chamber of Parliament," a bench of Chief Justice Surya Kant and Justices Joymalya Bagchi and V Mohana said while refusing to entertain a petition seeking quashing of a notification reserving Kadipur assembly constituency in UP for SCs.

The CJI-led bench said identification of constituencies to reserve them for SCs or STs was the sole prerogative of the legislature and the court could not interfere in it, and suggested the petitioner could resort to protests to make elected representatives take corrective measures.
The bench, which has been dealing with a large number of petitions on CJP protests, said in a lighter vein, "It is a good season for protest, dharna and 'naare baji'.

You can also raise your voice (in protest) and tell the elected representatives that time is ripe for revising the criteria of reserving constituencies for the SC community and adopt the principle of rotational reservation.
By approaching the constitutional court, you have dialled a wrong number.

"Appearing for a petitioner, senior advocate Gagan Gupta questioned the manner in which constituencies were geographically identified and reserved for SCs and asked whether "Section 9(1)(c) of the Delimitation Act, 2002, can constitutionally operate in a manner which permits the same territorial constituencies to remain reserved for SCs over successive electoral cycles without any mechanism for periodic rotation".
The bench said, "Delimitation is a legislative exercise and the guidelines for carrying out that exercise cannot be tweaked by the courts.

Can the judiciary mandate the Delimitation Commission to adopt rotational reservation policy while demarcating constituencies for SCs?" The SC agreed with Allahabad HC, which had said that since Articles 330 and 332 provide for reserving constituencies for SCs and STs, no general candidate could claim that his right to contest from constituencies reserved for SCs and STs was violated.
